en: Vimānavatthu: The Mansion of the Man,
Chapter on Well-Placed [Offerings]
6. The Story of the Cowherd’s Mansion Having seen the god in his lofty mansion that has long endured, the monk questioned him:
With hand-ornaments fastened,
glorious as the moon in a celestial mansion,
adorned, wearing garlands, and well-robed.
Wearing earrings, with hair and beard trimmed,
adorned with hand-ornaments, and glorious,
he was like the moon in a celestial mansion.
And celestial lutes play sweetly,
performed by eightfold groups of well-trained and beautiful beings;
and celestial maidens, noble dwellers of the Thirty-three, [dwell there].
They dance, sing, and rejoice.
You have attained the power of a deva and possess great majesty;
what merit did you perform while being a human?
“By what means have you come to possess such blazing majesty,
and why does your radiance illuminate all directions?
That son of the gods, being delighted, [replied:]
the fruit of which action is this:
"I, having become a human among humans..."
"I went there to guard the cows of others;
then a recluse came into my presence,
and the cattle went off to graze for a month."
"Both what must be done and what ought to be performed"—
thus, venerable sir, did I reflect at that time; and then,
having gained right mindfulness through wise attention, I thought:
"I give it, O Bhante," I said, and I cast away that which is endless.
Hurriedly, I departed from the field of the month,
lest this wealth of his should be destroyed.
Then a black snake of great venom bit my foot as I was hurrying;
thus I am afflicted with pain and oppressed by suffering.
The bhikkhu himself released that endless [coil] and,
out of compassion for me, took the rice porridge;
having passed away from there, I am now a deity.
That very same wholesome deed was performed by me,
and I myself experience the happiness resulting from that deed;
for I have been greatly favored by you, O Venerable One.
Out of gratitude, I pay homage to you.
In this world with its devas and Māras,
there is no other sage who is as compassionate as you.
For you, O Venerable One, have shown me great compassion;
out of gratitude, I pay homage to you.
Whether in this world or in the next, [may you be well].
"There is no other sage more compassionate than you;
for you, O Blessed One, have shown me great compassion.
Out of gratitude, I pay homage to you."
The Gopālavimāna is the sixth.
